readings.title: Tableau
readings.challenge: Explain how paired images describe a friendship that onlookers condemn.
readings.focus: Two boys, one Black and one white, walk arm in arm past disapproving neighbours.
readings.context: Countee Cullen (1903–1946) grew up in Harlem and published Color, his first book of poems, in 1925, while still a student at New York University. A tableau is a striking scene, like a picture held still. Donald Duff, to whom the poem is dedicated, was a white friend of Cullen’s. “Sable” means black; in the 1920s friendships across the colour line drew stares and anger from both sides.

excerpt.locator: “Tableau,” the whole poem with its dedication; opens “_For Donald Duff_”; closes “…and see no wonder That lightning brilliant as a sword Should blaze the path of thunder.”.

questions.prompt: How do the two groups of onlookers react, and what is surprising about their reactions?
facilitatorNotes: Black neighbours stare from behind lowered blinds; white neighbours talk openly, “indignant.” Both disapprove, so the boys are judged from both sides of the colour line, not only by one. The poem shows prejudice as something a whole street shares.
evidence:
From lowered blinds the dark folk stare,
And here the fair folk talk,

Indignant that these two should dare
In unison to walk.

questions.prompt: What do the comparisons to day and night, and to lightning and thunder, suggest about the two boys?
facilitatorNotes: Each pair belongs together: day and night make one whole turn of time, and lightning goes with thunder. The images present the boys as partners in a natural order, not opposites. Readers may notice that each comparison gives both boys beauty and pride.
evidence:
The golden splendor of the day,
The sable pride of night.

That lightning brilliant as a sword
Should blaze the path of thunder.

questions.prompt: The boys “see no wonder” in their friendship. Why does the poem stress that they do not notice the stares?
facilitatorNotes: To them walking together is simply natural; the “wonder” exists only in the onlookers’ eyes. Their calm makes the neighbours look small. The dedication suggests Cullen drew on his own friendship, though the poem speaks for any such pair.
evidence:
Oblivious to look and word
They pass, and see no wonder

readings.title: Heritage
readings.challenge: Hold a long poem’s contradictions in mind: a speaker who denies a feeling while showing it.
readings.focus: A young Black American asks what Africa means to him and cannot settle the answer.
readings.context: Countee Cullen (1903–1946) grew up in Harlem and published Color, his first book of poems, in 1925, while still a student at New York University. Harold Jackman, to whom the poem is dedicated, was Cullen’s close friend. “Three centuries removed” means the speaker’s ancestors were brought from Africa as slaves about three hundred years earlier. A juggernaut is a huge, unstoppable force; to “doff” is to take off; corollas are the petals of a flower; “heathen” means not Christian; the “twice-turned cheek” recalls Jesus’s teaching to turn the other cheek.
readings.contentNote: The poem draws on the 1920s picture of Africa as “jungle” and “barbaric,” which the speaker both repeats and struggles with. It questions the picture of Christ as white, and a few lines describe dancing and lovers.

excerpt.locator: “Heritage,” the whole poem with its dedication; opens “(_For Harold Jackman_)”; closes “…_Not yet has my heart or head_ _In the least way realized_ _They and I are civilized._”.

questions.prompt: In the third stanza the speaker calls Africa “a book one thumbs / Listlessly.” How do the stanzas that begin “So I lie” contradict that?
facilitatorNotes: He claims Africa bores him, yet he cannot shut out the drums even with his thumbs in his ears, and the rain makes him “twist and squirm.” “So I lie” can mean he lies awake, and also that he tells a lie: the claim of indifference is not true. Readers can decide which meaning is stronger.
evidence:
Africa? A book one thumbs
Listlessly, till slumber comes.

So I lie, who always hear,
Though I cram against my ear
Both my thumbs, and keep them there,
Great drums throbbing through the air.

questions.prompt: The poem’s Africa is full of jungles, drums and “wild barbaric birds.” Where might the speaker’s picture come from?
facilitatorNotes: He is “three centuries removed” and has never seen Africa, so his images come from books and the stereotypes of his time, as his own phrase about thumbing a book admits. The poem is partly about the gap between a real heritage and the pictures others have given him. Students should notice the stereotypes without assuming the poem simply believes them.
evidence:
_One three centuries removed_
_From the scenes his fathers loved,_

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker wish that the Christ he serves were black, and why does he ask forgiveness?
facilitatorNotes: A Black Christ would share his people’s suffering, a “kindred woe” that would guide him. Having dismissed African gods made by human hands, he admits he too fashions “dark gods,” and fears this is a “human creed.” He plays a “double part,” loyal to his faith and longing for it to include him.
evidence: Wishing He I served were black,

Lord, forgive me if my need
Sometimes shapes a human creed.

questions.prompt: What does the final stanza admit about the speaker’s struggle?
facilitatorNotes: He must keep cooling his pride and blood “all day long and all night through,” afraid a hidden fire will burn. The last lines say he has not yet “realized” that he is “civilized,” which can be heard as sad, as ironic about what “civilized” means, or as an honest admission that the conflict is unresolved.
evidence:
_Quench my pride and cool my blood,_
_Lest I perish in the flood._
They and I are civilized.

readings.title: Seven epitaphs
readings.challenge: Find the twist in a very short poem, and explain how a few lines can judge a whole life.
readings.focus: Comic, sharp verses imagined for the gravestones of seven kinds of people.
readings.context: Countee Cullen (1903–1946) grew up in Harlem and published Color, his first book of poems, in 1925, while still a student at New York University. An epitaph is a short verse for a gravestone; these are imaginary ones written for types of people. A cherub is a child angel; an anarchist rejects all government; in the Bible, Samson killed a thousand men with a donkey’s jawbone and drew his strength from his uncut hair; “adamantine” means unbreakable; “Open Sesame” opens the robbers’ cave in the tale of Ali Baba; a death’s-head is a skull and crape is black cloth worn in mourning.
readings.contentNote: These are comic verses about death. “For a Lady I Know” mocks a white woman who imagines Black people as servants even in heaven.

excerpt.locator: Epitaphs, seven poems from “For a Lady I Know” to “For a Pessimist”; opens “SHE even thinks that up in heaven Her class lies late and snores, While poor black…”; closes “…a hat, Calamity his cape, While on his face a death’s-head sat And waved a bit of crape.”.

questions.prompt: What does the lady in “For a Lady I Know” believe about heaven, and what does the epitaph reveal about her?
facilitatorNotes: She imagines that her own class sleeps late in heaven while “poor black cherubs” do the chores. In four lines Cullen exposes her snobbery and racism: she cannot picture even heaven without servants. “She even thinks” makes the reader share the speaker’s amazement.
evidence:
SHE even thinks that up in heaven
Her class lies late and snores,
While poor black cherubs rise at seven
To do celestial chores.

questions.prompt: How can one epitaph serve for an evolutionist and his opponent?
facilitatorNotes: Death “proves” both were right: the body returns to “primal clay,” as the evolutionist expected, and the soul rises, as his religious opponent believed. The joke is that two men who argued all their lives end up agreeing. Readers can say whether the poem takes a side.
evidence:
SHOWING that our ways agreed,
Death is proof enough;

questions.prompt: Choose two other epitaphs. How does each one’s last line or image turn the joke, and which one is the harshest?
facilitatorNotes: The atheist now begs mountains to hide him from God’s “reproachful eyes”; the magician meets a door with no magic word; the pessimist wore his coffin as a hat all his life; the anarchist’s storming could not break death’s law; the “lovely lady” should not be dug up. Answers will differ; students should point to the turn in the final line.
evidence:
Hide me from the stabbing pain
In His reproachful eyes.

Now am barred behind a door
That has no “Open Sesame.”

readings.title: Judas Iscariot
readings.challenge: Recognise when a poet is openly reimagining a well-known story, and judge his reasons.
readings.focus: A ballad that asks us to see the disciple who betrayed Jesus as a loving friend.
readings.context: Countee Cullen (1903–1946) grew up in Harlem and published Color, his first book of poems, in 1925, while still a student at New York University. In the Gospels, Judas Iscariot is the disciple who betrayed Jesus to the authorities for thirty pieces of silver, identifying him with a kiss, and later hanged himself. Cullen, the son of a Harlem minister, retells the story in ballad stanzas. A lute is a stringed instrument; a tryst is a meeting; “under ban” means condemned.
readings.contentNote: The poem retells the betrayal of Jesus and refers to Judas’s suicide. It changes the Gospel story deliberately.

excerpt.locator: “Judas Iscariot,” the whole poem; opens “I THINK when Judas’ mother heard His first faint cry the night That he was born, that…”; closes “…little Jewish lad Who gave young Christ heart, soul, and limb, And all the love he had.”.

questions.prompt: The speaker keeps saying “I think” and “perhaps.” What kind of story is he telling?
facilitatorNotes: An imagined one: he fills in what the Gospels leave out, Judas’s birth, his mother’s love, his childhood with Jesus. The hedges admit that this is the speaker’s version, not scripture, and invite the reader to consider it rather than accept it.
evidence:
I THINK when Judas’ mother heard
His first faint cry the night
I think he knew the growing Christ,

questions.prompt: In this poem, why does Judas betray Jesus? How is that different from the usual story?
facilitatorNotes: Christ asks him to: it is the task assigned to him, as feeding the sheep is assigned to Peter, so that the plan of salvation can be fulfilled. Judas accepts “the sorry part” out of love, knowing he will be scorned. The usual story blames greed; here the thirty coins become a “monstrous weight” of pain, not a prize.
evidence:
Then, Judas, you must kill
One whom you love, One who loves you
So Judas took the sorry part,

questions.prompt: How does the speaker want us to remember Judas? Why might a poet choose to defend the most hated figure in the story?
facilitatorNotes: As “the little Jewish lad” who gave Jesus all his love, not as a traitor. Defending the despised fits a poet who writes elsewhere about people judged unfairly. Some readers will find the poem merciful and moving; others will object that it rewrites a sacred story. The poem’s direct appeal to “you … friend” asks each reader to choose.
evidence:
But I would rather think of him
As the little Jewish lad

readings.title: In Memory of Col. Charles Young
readings.challenge: Connect an elegy’s images to the history behind it.
readings.focus: A lament for a Black officer denied his command, ending in a prophecy.
readings.context: Countee Cullen (1903–1946) grew up in Harlem and published Color, his first book of poems, in 1925, while still a student at New York University. Charles Young (1864–1922), born into slavery in Kentucky, was the third Black graduate of the U.S. Military Academy at West Point and the first Black colonel in the U.S. Army. In 1917, as America entered the First World War, the Army retired him on medical grounds, keeping him from a command in France; he rode on horseback from Ohio to Washington, D.C., to prove his fitness. He died in 1922 in Lagos, Nigeria, while serving as a military attaché in West Africa, and was first buried there. An elegy is a poem of mourning.
readings.contentNote: The poem mourns a soldier held back by racial discrimination.

excerpt.locator: “In Memory of Col. Charles Young,” the whole poem; opens “ALONG the shore the tall, thin grass That fringes that dark river, While sinuously soft…”; closes “…that work below; From your rich dust and slaughtered will A tree with tongues will grow.”.

questions.prompt: Where does the poem place Young’s grave? Which details show it is far from America?
facilitatorNotes: Beside “that dark river,” with tom-toms throbbing above it and the hills “weird with light”: Africa, where he died. The setting connects him to the continent of his ancestors. Readers might discuss whether the African images honour him or exoticise the place.
evidence: Above your grave the tom-toms throb,

questions.prompt: What might the “honeyed lies” be, and what happens to them at the “great dark heart”?
facilitatorNotes: Sweet-sounding official reasons and flattery, like the medical excuse that kept him from command. At the great heart of grief, drained bitter like a well, the lies find nothing to drink and “die.” The image says that mourning sees through the excuses.
evidence:
And all the honeyed lies they tell
Come there to thirst and die.

questions.prompt: What does the final image, “a tree with tongues,” promise?
facilitatorNotes: His “slaughtered will,” the ambition that was killed, becomes roots no lie can kill, and from his dust a tree will grow that speaks: his story will be told by those who come after. The poem turns grief into a prophecy of remembrance. Readers may see the tree as later generations of Black soldiers, writers, or both.
evidence:
No lie is strong enough to kill
The roots that work below;
A tree with tongues will grow.

readings.title: Atlantic City Waiter
readings.challenge: Find the mask in a poem and what shows through it, and question the poem’s explanation.
readings.focus: A waiter whose grace and hidden pride the diners cannot stop watching.
readings.context: Countee Cullen (1903–1946) grew up in Harlem and published Color, his first book of poems, in 1925, while still a student at New York University. Atlantic City is a seaside resort in New Jersey, known then for its grand hotels. Viands are fine foods; dexterous means skilful; artifice is deliberate pretence; acquiescent means quietly accepting; a cask is a barrel.
readings.contentNote: The poem traces the waiter’s grace to “ten thousand years on jungle clues,” an idea about race that many readers now question.

excerpt.locator: “Atlantic City Waiter,” the whole poem; opens “WITH subtle poise he grips his tray Of delicate things to eat; Choice viands to their…”; closes “…Of bland gentility, The jungle flames like a copper cask Set where the sun strikes free.”.

questions.prompt: What do the ladies watch, and how does Cullen describe the waiter’s movement?
facilitatorNotes: They stop with food halfway to their mouths to watch his feet, which “carve” paths through the crowded room. He is skilful and poised; the diners, not the waiter, are the ones distracted.
evidence: Choice viands to their mouths half way, The ladies watch his feet
Go carving dexterous avenues Through sly intricacies;

questions.prompt: “For him to be humble who is proud / Needs colder artifice.” What is the waiter hiding, and does the hiding work?
facilitatorNotes: He is proud but must act humble for his customers, and that takes cold, deliberate pretence. He gives up “half his pride,” yet “In vain”: his real self still blazes through the “mask / Of bland gentility.”
evidence: For him to be humble who is proud Needs colder artifice;
Though half his pride is disavowed, In vain the sacrifice.
Sheer through his acquiescent mask

questions.prompt: Twice the poem uses “jungle” to explain the waiter. What is Cullen claiming, and do you accept it?
facilitatorNotes: He credits the waiter’s grace and fire to a long African past, meaning it as pride. But it rests on a stereotype: that Black people’s talents are inherited and “primitive” rather than skill and character. The closing image, a copper cask flashing in the sun, is striking either way. Readers can admire the image and still question the idea.
evidence: Ten thousand years on jungle clues Alone shaped feet like these.
The jungle flames like a copper cask Set where the sun strikes free.

readings.title: Two Who Crossed a Line (She Crosses)
readings.challenge: Read a community’s feelings through the voice that tells the story.
readings.focus: A light-skinned woman leaves to live as white, and one day returns.
readings.context: Countee Cullen (1903–1946) grew up in Harlem and published Color, his first book of poems, in 1925, while still a student at New York University. “Crossing the line,” or passing, meant that a light-skinned person of Black ancestry lived as white, often cutting off family and friends, to escape segregation. The book prints two poems under this title; this first one is about a woman. A shade can mean a ghost, or the shadow of someone’s former self.

excerpt.locator: “Two Who Crossed a Line,” the first of the two poems under that title, “She Crosses”; opens “(_She Crosses_)”; closes “…no word asked, gave none; Only the silence in her face Said seats were dear in the sun.”.

questions.prompt: Why does she cross the line? What does the poem suggest about what she wanted and what stopped her?
facilitatorNotes: She craved a certain “air,” perhaps freedom and opportunity, but where she stood it was spoiled; it was “too much to bear.” She “braved / Her gods,” defying her community’s loyalties. The poem does not say exactly what the “smell of pine” means, so readers can suggest readings (the South, the poverty of her surroundings, danger).
evidence: FROM where she stood the air she craved Smote with the smell of pine;
It was too much to bear; she braved Her gods and crossed the line.

questions.prompt: Who is “we”? How do their feelings about her change?
facilitatorNotes: Her own people, the community she left. First they are hurt, then envious, then they forget her name. Each stage shows a different way of coping with someone who has left you behind.
evidence: And we were hurt to see her go,
We envied her a while,
Then we forgot her name,

questions.prompt: When she comes back, what has happened to her? What does her silence say?
facilitatorNotes: She returns calm but “Sorrow-proud and sorrow-wise,” with “trouble” at her breast: life on the other side has hurt her. She asks nothing and explains nothing. Her face says “seats were dear in the sun”: a place in the white world cost her dearly (“dear” means both expensive and precious). Readers can infer what happened; the poem refuses to tell.
evidence: With trouble sucking at her breast,
Only the silence in her face Said seats were dear in the sun.

readings.title: Pagan Prayer
readings.challenge: Hear a challenge inside a prayer.
readings.focus: A doubter prays for his people’s faith, and questions God.
readings.context: Countee Cullen (1903–1946) grew up in Harlem and published Color, his first book of poems, in 1925, while still a student at New York University. A pagan here means someone outside the Christian faith. Land left “fallow” is left unplanted for a season; credulity is readiness to believe; “turn the other cheek” is Christ’s teaching not to strike back; plaints are laments; to “compass” is to win over.
readings.contentNote: The speaker asks whether his people are God’s “bastard kin,” children shut out of the family.

excerpt.locator: “Pagan Prayer,” the whole poem; opens “NOT for myself I make this prayer, But for this race of mine That stretches forth from…”; closes “…Retrieve my race again; So shall you compass this black sheep, This pagan heart. Amen.”.

questions.prompt: For whom does the speaker pray? How is he different from them?
facilitatorNotes: Not for himself but for his race. They are humble believers who turn the other cheek; he is restless, doubting, and pays “debts in kind.” “Bless their credulity” can be read as tender or as faintly mocking; readers can decide.
evidence: NOT for myself I make this prayer, But for this race of mine
But these are humble and believe; Bless their credulity.

questions.prompt: “Our Father, God; our Brother, Christ, / Or are we bastard kin.” What accusation does this question make?
facilitatorNotes: If God is Father and Christ is Brother, why are Black people’s prayers unheard and the doors “barred from within”? The speaker asks whether they are treated as illegitimate children. The prayer turns into a challenge to God, and to Christians who teach the words but do not live them.
evidence: Their kinship seems a little thing Who sorrow all the day.
Or are we bastard kin, That to our plaints your ears are closed,

questions.prompt: What bargain does the last stanza offer? Is the poem finally an act of faith or of defiance?
facilitatorNotes: If God “retrieves” his race, God will win back this “black sheep” as well; the phrase plays on the family stray and on his colour. It is a prayer, so in one sense faithful, but it sets terms. Readers may argue for faith, defiance, or both.
evidence: Retrieve my race again; So shall you compass this black sheep, This pagan heart. Amen.

readings.title: To My Fairer Brethren
readings.challenge: Explain a complaint made in the language of sport and games.
readings.focus: A speaker who must win three times over to be believed.
readings.context: Countee Cullen (1903–1946) grew up in Harlem and published Color, his first book of poems, in 1925, while still a student at New York University. “Fairer” here means lighter-skinned, and “brethren” means brothers. “Treble” means three times; to catch someone “on the hip” is to have him at a disadvantage. Wreaths of laurel were once prizes for poets and athletes; “rakishly” means at a jaunty angle.

excerpt.locator: “To My Fairer Brethren,” the whole poem; opens “THOUGH I score you with my best, Treble circumstance Must confirm the verdict, lest It be…”; closes “…my wreaths a bit Rakishly and proud, I have bought my right to it; Let it be allowed.”.

questions.prompt: What must the speaker do for his win to be accepted? Put the first two stanzas in your own words.
facilitatorNotes: Beating his white rivals once is not enough; it would be called luck. He needs “treble circumstance” to prove it, and matching them is “insufficient”: he must beat them decisively. It describes a double standard: a Black achiever has to be far better to be counted equal.
evidence: THOUGH I score you with my best, Treble circumstance Must confirm the verdict, lest It be laid to chance.
Insufficient that I match you Every coin you flip;

questions.prompt: Why does he feel entitled to wear his wreaths “Rakishly and proud”? Would you call it arrogance?
facilitatorNotes: He has paid more for each prize than anyone else, so he has “bought” the right to enjoy it. Critics might call it arrogance; he answers in advance that his pride is earned. Readers can weigh whether pride is fair when the contest was not.
evidence: Should I wear my wreaths a bit Rakishly and proud, I have bought my right to it;

questions.prompt: He calls his rivals “brethren” and ends “Let it be allowed.” What tone does he take with them?
facilitatorNotes: Polite on the surface, even brotherly, but sharp underneath. “Let it be allowed” can be a request or a quiet demand. The short, neat stanzas make the complaint sound controlled, which makes it harder to dismiss.
evidence: Let it be allowed.
Your demand is that I catch you Squarely on the hip.

readings.title: The Shroud of Color
readings.challenge: Follow a long dream-vision stage by stage and explain what finally changes the speaker’s mind.
readings.focus: A young man in despair over his colour is shown visions until he chooses to live.
readings.context: Countee Cullen (1903–1946) grew up in Harlem and published Color, his first book of poems, in 1925, while still a student at New York University. A shroud is the cloth wrapped round a body for burial. In the Bible, Joseph’s father gives him a coat of many colours, and God provides a ram caught in a bush so that Abraham need not sacrifice his son. Lucifer is the angel who rebelled against God and fell; Gabriel, Michael and Raphael are archangels. To incarnadine is to stain red; a chimera is a wild fancy; an abattoir is a slaughterhouse; a recreant is a coward. The poem is dedicated to Llewellyn Ransom.
readings.contentNote: The speaker, crushed by racism, begs God to let him die; visions of struggle, war in heaven and his people’s suffering in slavery bring him to choose life.

excerpt.locator: “The Shroud of Color,” the whole poem with its dedication; opens “(_For Llewellyn Ransom_)”; closes “…though the tears for joy would run, My sight was clear; I looked and saw the rising sun.”.

questions.prompt: In his opening speech, why does the speaker want to die? What has he loved, and why does he think death would protect it?
facilitatorNotes: Being dark, he is “as dirt / Beneath my brother’s heel,” and every simple joy is spoiled. He has loved beauty and dreams, “a many-colored coat of dreams.” Now that he sees the truth about how men treat him, he fears it will destroy those dreams, so he would rather die and keep them pure.
evidence: Lord, being dark, forewilled to that despair My color shrouds me in, I am as dirt Beneath my brother’s heel;
Who wore a many-colored coat of dreams,
To dream still pure all that I loved, and die.

questions.prompt: What does each early vision show him: the struggling seed and rose, then men fighting, then the war in heaven? Why does he still resist?
facilitatorNotes: Everything alive struggles to live; even a rose seems to call him “Coward!” Men fight their way up a ladder; even God wins only at a cost, and Lucifer falls clutching stars. He answers that others can fight, since their “flesh is fair,” and asks “Am I a god?” He still believes his colour excuses him from the fight.
evidence: There was no thing alive save only I That held life in contempt and longed to die.
And no thing died that did not give A testimony that it longed to live.
Well, let them fight;
A star’s a star although it burns in hell.

questions.prompt: What finally changes his mind?
facilitatorNotes: The music of his own people: first joyful, then the cry of slavery, yet with “faith in man” running through it. He realises that “being dark, and living through the pain / Of it, is courage more than angels have.” He is persuaded not by “fairer men” or by faith alone but by his own people’s endurance, and his private grief merges into theirs.
evidence: How being dark, and living through the pain Of it, is courage more than angels have.
Lord, I will live persuaded by mine own.
My spirit has come home, that sailed the doubtful seas.

questions.prompt: Compare the opening “Lord, being dark” with the ending. How has his feeling about his colour and his dreams changed? Is the turn convincing?
facilitatorNotes: At first his colour is a shroud; at the end he is “Glad of the blood in my smallest vein,” keeps a “loyal dream,” and vows to “match” it to truth. He sees clearly and the sun is rising. Some readers find the turn earned by the vision of his people; others may find it sudden. Either view should cite the poem.
evidence: Glad of the blood in my smallest vein,
Oh, I will match you yet,
My sight was clear; I looked and saw the rising sun.

readings.title: To John Keats, Poet. At Spring Time
readings.challenge: Follow a poem addressed to a poet who died a hundred years before it was written.
readings.focus: Spring overwhelms a young poet, who finds a dead poet alive in it.
readings.context: Countee Cullen (1903–1946) grew up in Harlem and published Color, his first book of poems, in 1925, while still a student at New York University. John Keats (1795–1821) was an English poet of beauty who died of tuberculosis at twenty-five. The poem is dedicated to the writer Carl Van Vechten; the note at its end, printed in the book, dates it “Spring, 1924.” A tocsin is an alarm bell; “The Vision Splendid” is a phrase from Wordsworth for the glory a child sees in the world; to “keep revel” is to celebrate.

excerpt.locator: “To John Keats, Poet. At Spring Time,” the whole poem with its dedication and the book’s note; opens “(_For Carl Van Vechten_)”; closes “[Footnote A: Spring, 1924]”.

questions.prompt: Why can the speaker not “hold my peace”? What does spring do to him?
facilitatorNotes: This spring is the most beautiful he has known, and he must speak. He is “helpless” in it, like a newborn lamb on unsteady legs, and everything that slept is awake. The repeated opening line shows a feeling that will not stay quiet.
evidence: There never was a spring like this;
I am as helpless in the toil Of Spring as any lamb that bleats

questions.prompt: Where does the speaker find John Keats now?
facilitatorNotes: In nature: Keats’s will pulses up the sap of a maple, his voice is in its leaves, his fingers “work as grass” on “the broad sweet page of the earth.” His body has become earth, and the earth is now his poem. So “John Keats still writes poetry.”
evidence: Is pulsing up some tremulous Sap road of a maple tree,
Of the night on the broad sweet page of the earth.
Know John Keats still writes poetry.

questions.prompt: The poem ends with people finding the speaker strange. Why does he not mind? What does the poem suggest about poets speaking to each other across time and difference?
facilitatorNotes: They see only a young man deranged by spring; he knows he has company. A young Black poet in Harlem claims an English poet of a century before as a fellow reveller: beauty and poetry belong to anyone who loves them. Readers might debate whether this is an escape from the world of his other poems or a claim to the whole tradition of poetry.
evidence: Folks seeing me must think it strange That merely spring should so derange My mind.
John Keats, keep revel with me, too.
